props.title: Eating Raoul

sections.content: Eating Raoul (1982) stands as Paul Bartel's wickedly satirical masterpiece of Reagan-era excess and moral hypocrisy. This pitch-black comedy follows the Blands, a prudish couple who discover they can fund their restaurant dreams by killing "swingers" and stealing their money. The film's brilliant intersection with other early 80s cult classics like Polyester (1981) and Liquid Sky (1982) captures a moment when independent cinema dared to skewer American materialism and sexual politics with gleefully perverse humor. Bartel's deadpan direction perfectly balances horror and hilarity.

sections.content: The film's influence ripples through later savage social satires like Serial Mom (1994) and American Psycho (2000), which similarly use murder as metaphor for class warfare and consumerist critique. Bartel's genius lies in making his murderous protagonists somehow sympathetic - they're prudes killing perverts to achieve the "American Dream" of small business ownership. The deadpan tone and matter-of-fact violence prefigure the Coen Brothers' style in films like Blood Simple (1984).

What makes Eating Raoul particularly fascinating is its positioning between exploitation cinema and art house fare. Like Pink Flamingos (1972), it uses shocking content to critique bourgeois values while maintaining a strangely wholesome core. The Blands aren't deviants - they're conservative squares using deviant means to achieve conventional ends. This tension between form and content, sleaze and respectability, makes the film uniquely subversive. SUBHEAD: Cultural Context and Legacy

sections.content: Eating Raoul emerged during a fertile period for independent cinema tackling taboo subjects. Films like Ms. 45 (1981) and Basket Case (1982) were pushing boundaries in grindhouse theaters while Polyester (1981) brought exploitation themes to art houses. Bartel's film uniquely bridges these worlds, maintaining midnight movie outrageousness while offering genuine social commentary about capitalism, sexuality, and class.
